opus-5.5.text:
I think a few things have come together at once. The first is that language models have gotten good enough at reasoning that they can actually propose meaningful steps in a proof. Not perfectly, but well enough that you can search over their suggestions and make real progress. A few years ago that just wasn't true.

The second is that the formal side has matured a lot. Lean in particular has a growing community and a large library, Mathlib, that encodes a huge amount of undergraduate and graduate math in a machine-checkable form. That matters enormously, because it gives you a perfect verifier. When the model claims it has proven something, you don't have to trust it. You check it, and the answer is either right or wrong. No hallucinations survive that check.

And that combination is really powerful. When you have a model that can generate candidate reasoning and a verifier that gives you a clean, reliable signal, you can do reinforcement learning at scale. The model tries things, the verifier tells it what worked, and you generate your own training data. You're not limited by how much human-written math exists on the internet. That's the key unlock for us. Math is one of the few domains where you can create essentially unlimited high-quality synthetic data, because correctness is objective.

Then there's the bigger picture. We think mathematical reasoning sits underneath a lot of what matters: software verification, physics, engineering, anything where you need to be sure something is correct. If you can build a system that reasons rigorously and verifiably, it isn't just a better calculator. It's a foundation for trustworthy AI more broadly. So it felt like the tools were finally ready, the approach was clear, and the payoff was enormous. That's why we started Harmonic when we did.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are really three things that came together at the same time, and any one of them alone wouldn't have been enough.

The first is Lean. For decades, formal verification was this niche thing that a few hundred people in the world did, and the tooling was painful. What's happened over the last five or six years with Lean and mathlib is that the mathematical community actually showed up. You now have a library of hundreds of thousands of formalized theorems covering a big chunk of an undergraduate and increasingly a graduate curriculum, written by actual mathematicians. That gives you a substrate to train on and, more importantly, a verifier that tells you with certainty whether a proof is correct. That didn't exist in a usable form ten years ago.

The second is that language models got good enough to do the informal part. If you'd tried this in 2018, the models couldn't reason through a competition problem in plain English, let alone write Lean. Now they can sketch a plausible argument, and the question becomes whether you can close the gap between the sketch and something a proof checker accepts. That's a search and reinforcement learning problem, and it's exactly the kind of problem where having a perfect reward signal matters.

And that's the third piece, which is really the thesis of the company. Most of the frustration people have with AI today comes down to hallucination. The model says something confidently and it's wrong, and there's no oracle to catch it. Mathematics is the one domain where you have that oracle for free. If the proof checks, it's correct, full stop. So you can let the model generate millions of attempts, verify every single one, and train only on what's actually true. You get a flywheel that's impossible in most other domains because the ground truth is so expensive to obtain.

So when I look at it, the question isn't really why now, it's why not sooner. The ingredients just weren't all there until recently. And I think the payoff goes well beyond math. If you can build a system that reasons reliably where correctness is checkable, you've learned a lot about how to make reasoning reliable in places where it isn't, like software, or eventually science and engineering. Math is where we can prove the approach works, in the literal sense.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things coming together. One is that language models have become good enough to give us useful intuition about how to approach a mathematical problem. The other is that formal proof systems give us a way to check that intuition precisely. You can propose a step and get definitive feedback about whether it’s valid, rather than asking another model whether it looks right.

That creates a really interesting learning loop. The model can try things, get feedback, and improve, with a much clearer signal than you have in many other domains. There’s still a lot of work to do, but that combination makes this feel like the right moment to tackle it.

And for us, the motivation goes beyond solving math problems. We want AI that can reason reliably. Mathematics gives us a place to develop that capability where we can actually verify the result.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a few things are coming together. Models have become much better at reasoning and writing code, and formal mathematics gives us a way to check whether their reasoning is actually correct. You can propose a proof, run it through a verifier, and get a definitive signal about whether it works. That’s a powerful foundation for training systems to improve.

The exciting thing is that you don’t have to rely entirely on people producing more examples. A system can attempt problems, get feedback, and learn from those attempts. There’s still a lot of hard work in making that loop effective, but the ingredients are there now in a way they weren’t a few years ago.

And mathematics is a great place to develop reliable reasoning. You can’t just give an answer that sounds persuasive; every step has to hold up. We think that’s an important capability to build, both for mathematics itself and for the broader applications that depend on it.
